messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rangi Parata is a 53-year-old Māori-New Zealander photographer who has lived in the United States for nearly two decades, building a respected career documenting conflict zones and humanitarian crises for international news outlets. He is married, and his wife has described watching him become, over the past three years, a man she barely recognizes — someone who cannot sit in a restaurant without first walking its perimeter, who calls her from assignment locations simply to hear her say that he is going to be fine. Rangi himself came to the intake appointment with his back against the wall of the waiting room, eyes moving steadily across the other patients.

Three years ago, while on assignment in a politically unstable region, Rangi was detained by a paramilitary faction and held for eleven days in a series of small rooms with other captives. The conditions were unpredictable in the way that made them most psychologically corrosive: guards rotated without pattern, meals arrived or did not, and violence was administered without discernible reason. What Rangi remembers most vividly is the way a guard would cross the room with a sudden, purposeful stride — the shift in posture that preceded something terrible — and the complete impossibility of knowing, when a door opened, whether it meant food or a beating. He was eventually released without explanation. He flew home. He told his wife he was fine and went back to work within a week.

The symptoms did not announce themselves dramatically. They accumulated. Within months of his return, Rangi found that he could not enter a location — a gallery opening, a press briefing, a coffee shop — without first identifying the exits and positioning himself where no one could approach from behind. In his professional life, this meant he began declining certain assignments: crowded press conferences, indoor events with poor sightlines. He told his editors it was a scheduling conflict. What he could not tell them was that he had stood outside a venue in downtown Chicago for twenty minutes, unable to make himself walk through the door, because he had not yet worked out where he would run if he needed to. His body, he said, simply would not cooperate — a persistent, low-grade muscular tension that he described as being permanently braced for impact, as though his nervous system had never received the signal that the detention had ended.

The constant sense that danger was present and imminent — that any person moving quickly nearby might be the beginning of something — drove Rangi toward a set of behaviors that felt, to him, entirely rational. He began choosing seats at the periphery of every room, back to the wall, facing the entrance; in restaurants, he would ask to be reseated if the host placed him elsewhere, and on one occasion left without eating because no suitable position was available. He scanned faces in public for signs of hostile intent, reading the body language of strangers with the same professional attention he had once reserved for the edges of conflict zones. And he sought reassurance — from his wife, from colleagues, from his physician — asking repeatedly whether they thought he seemed all right, whether they believed he was coping. He had come to believe that if he asked enough people and received enough confirmation, the feeling of threat might subside. It did not. In fact, the reassurance-seeking and the escape planning and the hypervigilant scanning had the effect of keeping the alarm alive: each time he mapped an exit or repositioned himself for safety, his body registered the action as evidence that danger was real and present, the tension never releasing, the monitoring never switching off. The loop had become self-sustaining — the strategies that were meant to lower the threat signal instead kept amplifying it, and the amplified threat made the strategies feel more necessary than ever.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was a conversation with his wife after he refused to attend their daughter's university graduation ceremony because he could not assess the auditorium in advance. He had sat in the car outside and wept. He told the intake clinician that he did not want to lose any more of his life to this. What he feared most was that the person who had walked into that room three years ago — curious, willing, unafraid — was simply gone.
